section_name: Overview and the long view
title: Evolution of the graphics processing unit (GPU)
why: IEEE Micro 41(6). The architects' own twenty-year retrospective, from G80 to Ampere: why unified shaders, why SIMT, why the datapath specialized. The best single companion to this deck.

section_name: Overview and the long view
title: The GPU computing era
why: IEEE Micro 30(2). The state of the art at Fermi's launch: the Tesla line from G80 to GF100, the programming model, and the case that GPUs had become general processors.

section_name: Overview and the long view
title: Understanding throughput-oriented architectures
why: CACM 53(11), open access. The clearest statement of the latency-versus-throughput framing that slide 2 uses: many threads, simple cores, wide memory.

section_name: Overview and the long view
title: A closer look at GPUs
why: CACM 51(10). A short, precise account of how a GPU core differs from a CPU core (SIMD lanes, multithreading, shared state), written as G80 and CUDA arrived.

section_name: Overview and the long view
authors: Owens, Houston, Luebke, Green, Stone and Phillips
title: GPU computing
why: Proceedings of the IEEE 96(5); open copy at escholarship.org/content/qt0cv1p1nc/qt0cv1p1nc.pdf. The survey written at the moment GPGPU became GPU computing: hardware, programming models, applications.

section_name: Overview and the long view
title: How GPUs work
why: IEEE Computer 40(2). A four-page primer on the pipeline and its programmable stages, for readers who need the graphics side of slides 5-6 explained from zero.

section_name: Overview and the long view
title: The History of the GPU: Steps to Invention
why: Springer, volume 1 of three. The pre-history: from early raster hardware to the first consumer 3D chips; dense with dates and die photographs.

section_name: Overview and the long view
title: The History of the GPU: Eras and Environment
why: Springer, volume 2. 3dfx to unified shaders; the industrial history behind the timeline on slide 4.

section_name: Overview and the long view
title: The History of the GPU: New Developments
why: Springer, volume 3. The 2010s and the turn to AI; overlaps the last third of this deck.

section_name: Overview and the long view
title: Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach, 6th edition, chapter 4 (data-level parallelism in vector, SIMD and GPU architectures)
why: Textbook. Chapter 4 unifies vector machines, SIMD extensions and GPUs in one vocabulary and works a Pascal example; the 5th edition (2011) does the same with Fermi.

section_name: The graphics pipeline, fixed and programmable
title: The Geometry Engine: a VLSI geometry system for graphics
why: SIGGRAPH 1982; open copy at web.stanford.edu/class/cs349g/p127-clark.pdf. The transform stage of the pipeline as a custom chip: the origin of fixed-function graphics hardware and of Silicon Graphics.

section_name: The graphics pipeline, fixed and programmable
title: RealityEngine graphics
why: SIGGRAPH 1993. SGI's high-end pipeline built from boards of Geometry Engines and raster chips; the fully fixed-function pipeline at its peak.

section_name: The graphics pipeline, fixed and programmable
title: Nvidia unveils GeForce 256 (August 31, 1999)
why: Press, secondary source. The launch coverage with NVIDIA's claims as made: 'nearly 23 million transistors', 480 Mpixels/s, and the coining of 'graphics processing unit'. Component databases list 17 M transistors.

section_name: The graphics pipeline, fixed and programmable
title: A user-programmable vertex engine
why: SIGGRAPH 2001. The GeForce 3's programmable vertex shader: the instruction set, the register model, and why the stage was made programmable. Slide 6.

section_name: The graphics pipeline, fixed and programmable
title: Cg: a system for programming graphics hardware in a C-like language
why: ACM TOG 22(3), SIGGRAPH 2003. The shading language that made shaders look like C and whose authors went on to CUDA; read with Kilgard's two-page summary, arXiv cs/0302013.

section_name: The graphics pipeline, fixed and programmable
title: Cg in two pages
why: A compact statement of the Cg programming model; the arXiv copy is the easiest to obtain.

section_name: The graphics pipeline, fixed and programmable
title: The GeForce 6800
why: IEEE Micro 25(2). The last large pre-unified NVIDIA design: separate vertex and pixel processors, Shader Model 3.0, and the load-balancing problem that G80 solved.

section_name: The graphics pipeline, fixed and programmable
title: Xbox 360 system architecture
why: IEEE Micro 26(2). The Xenos GPU (ATI, 2005), the first unified-shader design to ship, a year before G80.

section_name: The graphics pipeline, fixed and programmable
title: The Direct3D 10 system
why: SIGGRAPH 2006. The API side of unification: Shader Model 4.0's common shader core and why the fixed distinction between vertex and pixel programs was dropped.

section_name: The graphics pipeline, fixed and programmable
title: AMD's unified shader GPU history
why: Secondary source. Settles the 'first unified shader' question: Xenos first in a console (2005), G80 first on the PC with a common API (DirectX 10, 2006).

section_name: GPGPU and the unified G80 with CUDA
authors: Buck, Foley, Horn, Sugerman, Fatahalian, Houston and Hanrahan
title: Brook for GPUs: stream computing on graphics hardware
why: ACM TOG 23(3), SIGGRAPH 2004; project page graphics.stanford.edu/papers/brookgpu. Streams and kernels compiled to shaders: the programming model that CUDA's first author carried to NVIDIA. Slide 7.

section_name: GPGPU and the unified G80 with CUDA
authors: Owens, Luebke, Govindaraju, Harris, Krueger, Lefohn and Purcell
title: A survey of general-purpose computation on graphics hardware
why: Computer Graphics Forum 26(1); open copy at escholarship.org/content/qt9ns2d70c/qt9ns2d70c.pdf. The catalog of what ran on shaders before CUDA, and of the tricks (scatter via vertex processors, multi-pass reductions) that CUDA made unnecessary.

section_name: GPGPU and the unified G80 with CUDA
title: Using GPUs for machine learning algorithms
why: ICDAR 2005. The earliest paper training neural networks on a GPU, through the graphics API; three of the authors' ideas reappear in cuDNN a decade later.

section_name: GPGPU and the unified G80 with CUDA
title: High performance convolutional neural networks for document processing
why: IWFHR 2006, open access. Convolution unrolled into matrix multiply and run on a GPU: the formulation every later framework used.

section_name: GPGPU and the unified G80 with CUDA
title: NVIDIA Tesla: a unified graphics and computing architecture
why: IEEE Micro 28(2). The canonical G80 paper: streaming processors, the SM, SIMT (the term is introduced here), the memory system, and the graphics and compute pipelines sharing one array. Slides 8 and 11.

section_name: GPGPU and the unified G80 with CUDA
title: Scalable parallel programming with CUDA
why: ACM Queue 6(2), open access. The programming model as its designers explain it: threads, blocks, grids, shared memory, barriers, and why blocks are independent. Slide 9.

section_name: GPGPU and the unified G80 with CUDA
title: NVIDIA CUDA software and GPU parallel computing architecture (ISMM 2007 keynote)
why: The first appearance of CUDA's architecture in the academic literature, four months after the public beta.

section_name: GPGPU and the unified G80 with CUDA
title: Nvidia launches new architecture for its graphics chips (November 8, 2006)
why: Press, secondary source. Confirms that the GeForce 8800 and CUDA were announced on the same day.

section_name: GPGPU and the unified G80 with CUDA
title: Tesla product overview: C870, D870, S870 (June 2007)
why: Vendor datasheet. The first compute-only products: 128 thread processors, 1.5 GB, 76.8 GB/s, 'up to 518 gigaflops'.

section_name: GPGPU and the unified G80 with CUDA
title: The Khronos Group releases OpenCL 1.0 specification (press release, December 2008)
why: Vendor press release. The vendor-neutral standard with CUDA's model and different names (work-items, work-groups), six months after Apple's proposal.

section_name: GPGPU and the unified G80 with CUDA
title: Nvidia's GeForce 8800 graphics processor (launch review)
why: Press, secondary source. The launch-day architecture walkthrough with NVIDIA's briefing numbers, including the 185 W figure given to reviewers (155 W became the official maximum board power).

section_name: The CUDA model and its mapping to the chip
title: Programming Massively Parallel Processors: A Hands-on Approach, 3rd edition
why: Textbook. The course that goes with slides 9-10 and 14: the CUDA model, memory hierarchy, tiling, and performance considerations; the 4th edition (Hwu, Kirk and El Hajj, 2022) adds later architectures.

section_name: The CUDA model and its mapping to the chip
title: Optimizing parallel reduction in CUDA
why: Vendor tutorial, open. Seven versions of one kernel, each removing a specific inefficiency (divergence, bank conflicts, idle threads, instruction overhead); the single best introduction to GPU performance thinking.

section_name: The CUDA model and its mapping to the chip
title: Benchmarking GPUs to tune dense linear algebra
why: SC 2008 (Test of Time award, 2019), open copy. Microbenchmarks of G80 and GT200 used to design an SGEMM at 60% of peak; the register-blocking lesson every later GEMM followed.

section_name: The CUDA model and its mapping to the chip
title: Fermi GF100 GPU architecture
why: IEEE Micro 31(2). The Fermi SM of slide 10 described by its architects: dual warp schedulers, the configurable L1/shared array, the L2, ECC, and the graphics pipeline around them.

section_name: The CUDA model and its mapping to the chip
title: NVIDIA's next generation CUDA compute architecture: Fermi (whitepaper v1.1)
why: Vendor whitepaper (mirror; the nvidia.com original is the same document). The G80/GT200/Fermi comparison table, the SM diagram, the memory hierarchy and the 48 warps per SM that slide 10 quotes.

section_name: The CUDA model and its mapping to the chip
title: NVIDIA's Fermi: the first complete GPU computing architecture
why: Analyst whitepaper commissioned by NVIDIA; secondary source. Places Fermi against CPUs and earlier GPUs with unusual clarity about what 'general-purpose' required.

section_name: SIMT, latency hiding and the energy argument
title: Dynamic warp formation and scheduling for efficient GPU control flow
why: MICRO 2007, open copy. The first academic analysis of branch divergence in SIMT and a hardware proposal to regroup threads across warps; the cost model of slide 11.

section_name: SIMT, latency hiding and the energy argument
title: An analytical model for a GPU architecture with memory-level and thread-level parallelism awareness
why: ISCA 2009. The MWP/CWP model: how many warps a memory system can serve at once and how many the compute pipeline needs; the formal version of slide 12.

section_name: SIMT, latency hiding and the energy argument
authors: Bakhoda, Yuan, Fung, Wong and Aamodt
title: Analyzing CUDA workloads using a detailed GPU simulator
why: ISPASS 2009, open copy. GPGPU-Sim, the simulator most GPU architecture research used for a decade, and its first findings on interconnect and memory bottlenecks.

section_name: SIMT, latency hiding and the energy argument
title: Cache-conscious wavefront scheduling
why: MICRO 2012, open copy. Why more resident warps can hurt: L1 thrashing, and a scheduler that limits the active set; the counterpoint to maximal occupancy.

section_name: SIMT, latency hiding and the energy argument
title: Better performance at lower occupancy (GTC 2010 talk)
why: Vendor conference slides, secondary source. Instruction-level parallelism within a thread as a substitute for thread-level parallelism; the argument slide 12 summarizes.

section_name: SIMT, latency hiding and the energy argument
title: Understanding latency hiding on GPUs (PhD thesis, UC Berkeley EECS-2016-143)
why: Open access. The rigorous version of Little's law for GPUs, measured on Fermi through Maxwell; the reference for anyone modeling occupancy.

section_name: SIMT, latency hiding and the energy argument
authors: Keckler, Dally, Khailany, Garland and Glasco
title: GPUs and the future of parallel computing
why: IEEE Micro 31(5), open copy (DOI 10.1109/MM.2011.89). The energy tables behind slide 13: 50 pJ per double-precision FMA at 40 nm, 14 pJ per 64-bit SRAM read, 240 fJ per bit-millimeter of wire, 28-45 pJ per bit of DRAM access and interface, and the Echelon design that followed from them.

section_name: SIMT, latency hiding and the energy argument
authors: Esmaeilzadeh, Blem, St. Amant, Sankaralingam and Burger
title: Dark silicon and the end of multicore scaling
why: ISCA 2011. At fixed power only part of a chip can be active; the argument for specialization that the tensor core later embodied.

section_name: SIMT, latency hiding and the energy argument
authors: Dennard, Gaensslen, Yu, Rideout, Bassous and LeBlanc
title: Design of ion-implanted MOSFETs with very small physical dimensions
why: IEEE JSSC 9(5). The scaling law whose breakdown around 2005 ended clock-speed growth and made throughput architectures inevitable.

section_name: SIMT, latency hiding and the energy argument
title: A 30 year retrospective on Dennard's MOSFET scaling paper
why: IEEE SSCS Newsletter 12(1). Short, readable account of why the law stopped holding (leakage, threshold voltage) and what replaced it.

section_name: SIMT, latency hiding and the energy argument
title: Debunking the 100X GPU vs. CPU myth: an evaluation of throughput computing on CPU and GPU
why: ISCA 2010, open copy. Fourteen kernels tuned on both a GTX 280 and a Core i7-960: 2.5x on average. The paper that made honest comparisons the norm; slide 27.

section_name: The memory system and the roofline
title: Roofline: an insightful visual performance model for multicore architectures
why: CACM 52(4); open copy at escholarship.org/content/qt78h8v7mr/qt78h8v7mr.pdf. The model of slide 15: attainable performance as the minimum of peak and bandwidth times intensity.

section_name: The memory system and the roofline
title: Demystifying GPU microarchitecture through microbenchmarking
why: ISPASS 2010 (DOI 10.1109/ISPASS.2010.5452013), open technical-report copy. Pointer-chasing and dependent-chain measurements on GT200: about 440 cycles to global memory, 38 to shared memory, a 24-cycle arithmetic pipeline, the cache and TLB structure.

section_name: The memory system and the roofline
title: Dissecting GPU memory hierarchy through microbenchmarking
why: IEEE TPDS 28(1). The same method applied to Fermi, Kepler and Maxwell: cache sizes, set structure, latencies; fills the gap between Wong (GT200) and Jia (Volta).

section_name: The memory system and the roofline
title: JEDEC updates High Bandwidth Memory standard JESD235A (press release, January 12, 2016)
why: Standards body press release. HBM2: eight independent 128-bit channels per stack, up to 256 GB/s and 8 GB per stack, pseudo-channel mode; the memory of Pascal and Volta.

section_name: The memory system and the roofline
title: JEDEC announces publication of GDDR5X graphics memory standard JESD232 (January 21, 2016)
why: Standards body press release. The other 2016 path to bandwidth, used on the consumer GP104 instead of HBM2.

section_name: The memory system and the roofline
title: GeForce GTX 1080 whitepaper (GP104)
why: Vendor whitepaper (mirror). The consumer Pascal with GDDR5X; its comparison table is also the accessible source for GM204 (GTX 980) figures.

section_name: The generations: Tesla, Fermi, Kepler, Maxwell, Pascal
title: Tesla C1060 computing processor board specification (BD-04111-001_v06)
why: Vendor datasheet. GT200 as a compute product: 240 cores at 1.296 GHz, 4 GB GDDR3 at 102 GB/s, 187.8 W.

section_name: The generations: Tesla, Fermi, Kepler, Maxwell, Pascal
title: Tesla C2050 / C2070 GPU computing processor datasheet (July 2010)
why: Vendor datasheet. Fermi as shipped: 448 cores, 515 GFLOP/s double, 1.03 TFLOP/s single, 144 GB/s, 238 W.

section_name: The generations: Tesla, Fermi, Kepler, Maxwell, Pascal
title: NVIDIA's next generation CUDA compute architecture: Kepler GK110 (whitepaper v1.0)
why: Vendor whitepaper (mirror of the English document). The SMX, dynamic parallelism, Hyper-Q, GPUDirect RDMA, and the compute-capability table from Fermi to GK110.

section_name: The generations: Tesla, Fermi, Kepler, Maxwell, Pascal
title: Tesla K80 / K40 datasheet
why: Vendor datasheet (mirror). K40 at 4.29 / 1.43 TFLOP/s base and 5.04 / 1.68 boost; K80 at 8.74 / 2.91 with boost, 24 GB, 480 GB/s.

section_name: The generations: Tesla, Fermi, Kepler, Maxwell, Pascal
title: Tesla M40 datasheet (January 2016)
why: Vendor datasheet. Maxwell for training: 3,072 cores, 7 TFLOP/s with boost, 288 GB/s, 250 W, and the FP64 rate that kept it out of HPC.

section_name: The generations: Tesla, Fermi, Kepler, Maxwell, Pascal
title: NVIDIA Tesla P100 whitepaper (WP-08019-001_v01.1)
why: Vendor whitepaper (mirror of the same document). GP100 in full: the SM, FP16, HBM2 and CoWoS, NVLink 1.0, unified memory with page faulting, compute preemption, and Table 1 comparing K40, M40 and P100. Slide 20.

section_name: The generations: Tesla, Fermi, Kepler, Maxwell, Pascal
title: NVIDIA delivers massive performance leap for deep learning, HPC applications with NVIDIA Tesla P100 accelerators (press release, April 5, 2016)
why: Vendor press release. The launch claims as made: 5.3 / 10.6 / 21.2 TFLOP/s, 720 GB/s, 160 GB/s NVLink, 15.3 billion transistors.

section_name: The generations: Tesla, Fermi, Kepler, Maxwell, Pascal
title: Ultra-performance Pascal GPU and NVLink interconnect
why: IEEE Micro 37(2). GP100 and NVLink by their architects; the Hot Chips 28 talk by the same authors (old.hotchips.org, HC28.22.121) has the floorplan and PHY details.

section_name: The generations: Tesla, Fermi, Kepler, Maxwell, Pascal
title: New NVIDIA hyperscale accelerators boost machine learning throughput for web data centers (press release, November 10, 2015)
why: Vendor press release. The M40 announcement, and the moment NVIDIA named deep-learning training as a product category of its own.

section_name: The generations: Tesla, Fermi, Kepler, Maxwell, Pascal
title: ImageNet classification with deep convolutional neural networks
why: NIPS 2012, open access (also CACM 60(6), 2017). Trained 'between five and six days on two GTX 580 3GB GPUs'; the paper that redirected the architecture. Slide 19.

section_name: The generations: Tesla, Fermi, Kepler, Maxwell, Pascal
authors: Chetlur, Woolley, Vandermersch, Cohen, Tran, Catanzaro and Shelhamer
title: cuDNN: efficient primitives for deep learning
why: The library that tied every deep-learning framework to CUDA; convolution as GEMM with tiling in on-chip memory, the kernels the tensor core later accelerated.

section_name: The generations: Tesla, Fermi, Kepler, Maxwell, Pascal
title: Large-scale deep unsupervised learning using graphics processors
why: ICML 2009, open copy. Deep belief networks and sparse coding on a GTX 280: the first widely read case that GPUs change what deep learning can afford.

section_name: The generations: Tesla, Fermi, Kepler, Maxwell, Pascal
title: Deep, big, simple neural nets for handwritten digit recognition
why: Neural Computation 22(12). Plain multilayer perceptrons trained on GPUs beat the MNIST state of the art; evidence that compute, not cleverness, was the missing ingredient.

section_name: The generations: Tesla, Fermi, Kepler, Maxwell, Pascal
title: Nvidia GeForce GTX Titan X 12GB review (March 17, 2015)
why: Press, secondary source. The GM200 launch: 8 billion transistors, 601 mm2, 3,072 cores, FP64 at 1/32; the consumer die that became the Tesla M40.

section_name: Volta and the tensor core
title: NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU architecture (whitepaper WP-08608-001_v1.1)
why: Vendor whitepaper (mirror of the same document). The GV100 SM with its four processing blocks, tensor cores, independent thread scheduling, the unified L1/shared memory, NVLink 2.0, and Table 1 comparing P100 and V100. Slides 21-24.

section_name: Volta and the tensor core
title: Volta: performance and programmability
why: IEEE Micro 38(2). Volta by its architects: why the SM was repartitioned, how tensor cores fit the pipeline, and what independent thread scheduling cost and bought.

section_name: Volta and the tensor core
title: Tesla V100 data sheet (March 2018)
why: Vendor datasheet. SXM2 against PCIe: 7.8 / 15.7 / 125 against 7 / 14 / 112 TFLOP/s, 300 against 250 W, 16 or 32 GB.

section_name: Volta and the tensor core
title: Dissecting the NVIDIA Volta GPU architecture via microbenchmarking
why: Citadel's measurement of V100: 19-cycle shared memory, 28-cycle L1, about 193-cycle L2, 375-cycle global memory with a TLB hit and 1,029 with a miss, 4-cycle FP32 FMA, tensor-core behavior, and the instruction encoding. Slides 12 and 24.

section_name: Volta and the tensor core
authors: Markidis, Der Chien, Laure, Peng and Vetter
title: NVIDIA tensor core programmability, performance and precision
why: IPDPSW 2018. The WMMA API measured: achieved TFLOP/s against the 125 peak, and the precision lost to FP16 inputs with and without FP32 accumulation.

section_name: Volta and the tensor core
title: Mixed precision training
why: ICLR 2018. FP32 master weights, FP16 forward and backward passes, loss scaling; the recipe that made tensor cores usable for training without accuracy loss. Slide 23.

section_name: Volta and the tensor core
authors: NVIDIA (via Edge AI and Vision Alliance)
title: NVIDIA launches revolutionary Volta GPU platform (press release, May 10, 2017)
why: Vendor press release (mirror). The launch claims: 21 billion transistors, 640 tensor cores, 120 TFLOP/s (later 125), 900 GB/s.

section_name: Systems: interconnect, supercomputers, the alternatives
title: Pascal GPU with NVLink (Hot Chips 28 slides)
why: Conference slides, open. The GP100 floorplan, the HBM2 and CoWoS package, and the NVLink physical layer and the DGX-1 topology. Slide 25.

section_name: Systems: interconnect, supercomputers, the alternatives

section_name: Systems: interconnect, supercomputers, the alternatives

why: Press, secondary source. The DGX-2 and V100 32 GB announcement with the figures as given at GTC 2018.

section_name: Systems: interconnect, supercomputers, the alternatives

section_name: Systems: interconnect, supercomputers, the alternatives

section_name: Systems: interconnect, supercomputers, the alternatives
title: Swiss deploy world's fastest GPU-powered supercomputer
why: Benchmark-site news, secondary source. The Piz Daint P100 upgrade's timeline and node count.

section_name: Systems: interconnect, supercomputers, the alternatives
title: Larrabee: a many-core x86 architecture for visual computing
why: ACM TOG 27(3), SIGGRAPH 2008; open copy at courses.cs.washington.edu/courses/cse591n/08au/Papers/larrabee_manycore.pdf. The x86 alternative: many small cores, 16-wide vectors, coherent caches, graphics in software. Slide 27.

section_name: Systems: interconnect, supercomputers, the alternatives

why: Press, secondary source. Intel's December 4, 2009 statement that Larrabee would not ship as a discrete graphics product.

why: Vendor press release. The FirePro S9150: 2.53 TFLOP/s double, 5.07 single, 16 GB, 320 GB/s, 235 W; GCN hardware ahead of NVIDIA's on paper.

why: Secondary source. A short illustrated history of the Geometry Engine for readers who want the 1982 story in plain language.
